prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength where the lattice does not shift the clock transition, and for realizing it at a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, enabling millimetre-scale tests of gravitational redshift and sensitive searches for variation of constants

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and the round-1 exchange has made me more, not less, certain about the framing. The chair asked what is new relative to 2005 and 2012. My answer is narrow and I think it holds. The comb (2005) is a ruler that counts optical cycles. The 2012 prize recognised control of single trapped quantum systems, and the best ion clocks inherit a fundamental limit: one ion gives very little signal per cycle, so averaging to 1e-18 takes very long. The magic-wavelength lattice removes that trade-off. Thousands of atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free, and the light shift cancels between the clock states. That is Katori's idea (proposal and first strontium lattice spectroscopy around 2001-2005, as I recall it), and it is a new way of holding atoms while measuring them, not a better laser or a better comb. Ye's group then took the platform to systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18 and used it to resolve the gravitational redshift over a millimetre-scale height difference and to bound drifts of constants. On reproducibility, which I weight most as an experimentalist, JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE operate lattice clocks and their comparisons agree. Systematic shifts such as blackbody radiation and higher-order lattice effects were calculated and then checked experimentally, which is what separates a mature measurement from a claim. I agree with Lindroth that the citation should name what the clocks have shown, so that the prize is not read as one for an instrument alone. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and uses two of the three names available. I do not rely on the redefinition of the second, which is still pending, and the case would stand if that slipped by years.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is lineage and the nature of the result. A reader can say that after the comb and single-ion prizes this is an extraordinary refinement of an honoured lineage, and that nothing in nature was discovered, only a measurement made more precisely. Eriksson and Danielsson press this and I cannot dismiss it. I have not verified the primary-literature priority record: Lemonde and Wolf's lattice proposals, Hollberg, Gill and the ion-clock groups, NIST colleagues, and the Hg and Yb lattice clocks all contributed, so a two-name prize leaves real contributors out and the committee should expect that criticism. Part of Ye's profile sits in laser stabilisation and comb work, which is why the citation must rest on the lattice clock and its performance. Finally, the practical payoff is prospective, and if the committee values a new regime of matter more than a new regime of measurement, B009 is a legitimate competing choice.

responses.point: Olsson asked whether the lattice clock is a new door or a much better version of a door already opened, and asked that the record on who first demonstrated lattice clocks be checked.
responses.response: I cannot fully answer from memory, but the pattern I recall is this. The magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice spectroscopy of strontium come from Katori's group in Tokyo, and Lemonde and Wolf contributed concurrent theoretical analysis at SYRTE. JILA's role is the decisive demonstration that a many-atom lattice clock beats the single-ion fundamental limits in stability and reaches the 1e-18 regime. I read that as Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for making it the best clock, which is why the two-name split is defensible. On door versus better door: a clock limited by single-ion signal-to-noise could not average down to 1e-18 in practical times, and the lattice removed that limit. That is a new capability, and it is the capability that made millimetre-scale redshift measurements possible. I accept the lineage worry is real. Where I would not follow you is in treating it as disqualifying, provided the citation does not borrow from combs.

responses.point: Pearce asked what exactly is new relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, and said he would be comfortable if the answer is the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom stability gain.
responses.response: That is my answer, and I have written the citation so that it contains only that. The comb and the 2012 single-ion work are both necessary ingredients, the comb to count the optical cycles and the ion work to show what a well-isolated quantum system can do, but neither contains the idea of trapping an ensemble where the trap does not shift the transition. I also agree with you that B012 should not be paired with B049, since that would exceed three people. I will keep B012 as an alternative only. Your move from sixth place, based on colleagues' expertise, is a reasonable use of a committee, and I would add that the evidence you asked for, independent laboratories agreeing at the 1e-18 level, is in the published clock comparisons and not only in our say-so.

responses.point: Eriksson asked what physical discovery stands at the centre of the clock case, calling it a metrology achievement whose main scientific consequences are still to come, and favours B009 on the criterion of a verified new physical phenomenon.
responses.response: I think some of the consequences you call future are already in hand. The comparison of clocks at different heights resolves the gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale, which is a direct laboratory test of general relativity at a length scale no previous experiment reached. Limits on drifts of fundamental constants have also tightened because of these clocks. I will concede that this is a new capability, not a new particle or phase of matter. If your criterion is a new phenomenon in nature, B009 is the better fit, and I have it as my first alternative. My criterion is whether a measurement advance changed what can be observed, and I do not think the Nobel record says phenomena only: the 2005 and 2012 prizes were for methods. Where I would value your judgment is on reproducibility between groups of the correlated phase diagram, since that is the point that would most affect my view of B009.

responses.point: Olsson, Eriksson and Danielsson treat the unsettled pairing mechanism and the attribution gap (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Cao, Fatemi) as a manageable weakness for B009.
responses.response: I accept your argument that the pairing mechanism is a question about what comes after the door is open, and that a citation resting on flat bands and correlated insulators avoids it. My remaining concern is attribution rather than maturity. Three names cannot represent the earlier flat-band theory, the first-author experimentalists who did the hands-on work, or Dean's group, and the chair's question on this has not been answered by anyone. The clock configuration has a smaller attribution problem. This is why, in a choice between two strong candidates, I hold B049 first, and I would regard B009 as an acceptable result if the committee prefers a new regime of matter.

responses.point: Mehlig agreed that B012 is highly mature but hesitates to prefer it because the credit boundary among Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller, and possibly Jaksch is hard to defend, and said the cleanest framing would be quantum simulation of Hubbard physics.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning and with the framing. If the committee wants an atomic-physics prize built on quantum simulation, it should be written around Hubbard-model simulation with Mott-insulator and microscope demonstrations, and then Greiner belongs with Bloch and Zoller; Cirac would stay out only if the citation is experimental. Even so that is a decision the committee has not made, and it is a reason B012 remains my second alternative. I have moved B009 and B012 only in the sense that I now state clearly that B012 is the one I would defend if both B049 and B009 failed, because it is a mature field with decisive experiments. I have not changed my first choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct invention (many atoms, Doppler- and recoil-free, trap-induced shift cancelled) or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. This is a judgment about a lineage, and I cannot settle it with data.

Priority detail: I have not verified from the primary literature the dates and roles of Katori's proposal and first demonstration against Lemonde, Wolf, Hollberg, Gill and the Hg and Yb lattice groups, and a two-name prize will leave some of them out.
Whether the committee will weigh a measurement advance below a discovery of a new phenomenon, which is the central difference between B049 and B009.

Whether the correlated phase diagram of magic-angle graphene is reproducible between groups to the standard of the clock comparisons, and whether the attribution gap there can be closed within three names.
statement.conflict_note: As in round 1: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, the JILA group where Jun Ye (credited on B049) later worked. This was decades ago and I have no collaboration, financial tie or recent contact with Ye or Katori that I know of, and I do not regard it as grounds for recusal, but I note it for the record. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers and bears on B040, which is not in my configuration. My own work on rare-earth-ion crystals and laser stabilisation is adjacent to precision spectroscopy but has no credited-name connection to B049, B009 or B012. No new conflict has arisen since round 1.
